title: The Solar System And Earth'S Motions

sections.title: Formation and major constituents
sections.text:
The Solar System formed from a rotating cloud of gas and dust. Gravity concentrated most material into the young Sun, while the surrounding disk supplied particles that collided, accumulated and formed larger bodies. The properties of the disk varied with distance from the Sun, helping produce rocky inner planets and volatile-rich outer bodies.

The eight planets, outward from the Sun, are Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune. Mercury through Mars are terrestrial planets with rocky surfaces. Jupiter and Saturn are gas giants; Uranus and Neptune are often called ice giants because their bulk compositions differ from those of Jupiter and Saturn. These labels describe broad composition and structure, not a claim that their interiors consist of ordinary familiar ice throughout.

| Body | Distinguishing feature |
|---|---|
| Planet | Orbits the Sun, is approximately rounded by gravity, and has cleared its orbital neighbourhood under the astronomical classification |
| Dwarf planet | Approximately rounded and orbits the Sun but has not cleared its neighbourhood; is not a satellite |
| Asteroid | Small mainly rocky or metallic Solar System body |
| Comet | Small body with volatile material that can produce a coma and tails near the Sun |
| Meteoroid | Small natural object travelling through space |
| Meteor | Luminous atmospheric phenomenon produced by an incoming object |
| Meteorite | Material surviving passage to the ground |

The asteroid belt lies mainly between Mars and Jupiter. Many small icy bodies occur beyond Neptune. A comet's ion tail tends to point away from the Sun because of the solar wind, while its dust tail follows a more curved pattern affected by radiation pressure and orbital motion. A tail does not simply trail behind a comet like smoke behind a vehicle.

sections.title: Gravity and orbital motion
sections.text:
Gravity provides the inward acceleration needed to bend a planet's motion into an orbit. The planet's inertia carries it forward; gravity continually changes the direction of its velocity. An orbiting body is therefore in free fall rather than outside the influence of gravity.

Kepler's first law states that planetary orbits are ellipses with the Sun at one focus. The second states that the line joining a planet and the Sun sweeps equal areas in equal times, so orbital speed increases near perihelion and decreases near aphelion. The third relates orbital period to orbital size: for bodies orbiting the same dominant central mass, $T^2\propto a^3$, where $T$ is period and $a$ is semimajor axis.

For an ideal circular orbit, gravitational force $GMm/r^2$ supplies the centripetal force $mv^2/r$. Equating them gives $GMm/r^2=mv^2/r$, where $m$ is the orbiting mass. Cancelling $m$ and rearranging produces

$$v=\sqrt{\frac{GM}{r}}.$$

$v$ is orbital speed in metres per second, $G$ is the gravitational constant, $M$ is the central mass in kilograms and $r$ is orbital radius in metres measured from the centre. The orbiting object's mass cancels from the ideal relation. A smaller orbital radius around the same central body implies a higher circular speed.

sections.title: Rotation, revolution and seasons
sections.text:
Rotation is Earth's spinning around its axis. Revolution is its motion around the Sun. Rotation produces the daily alternation of light and darkness; revolution combined with axial tilt produces the annual cycle of seasons. Earth's axis is tilted by about 23.4 degrees relative to the perpendicular to its orbital plane.

When the Northern Hemisphere tilts toward the Sun, sunlight arrives more directly and daylight lasts longer. Both effects increase daily solar energy received and produce northern summer. The Southern Hemisphere then experiences winter. Six months later the geometry is reversed. Distance from the Sun is not the main cause: both hemispheres share essentially the same Earth–Sun distance at a given time yet experience opposite seasons.

At a solstice, the Sun reaches an extreme apparent northward or southward position. At an equinox, the Sun crosses the celestial equator and day and night are approximately equal, with small differences from refraction and the Sun's finite disk. At high latitudes, tilt can produce continuous summer daylight or winter darkness. Latitude, altitude, continentality and ocean currents further modify local climates.

sections.title: The Moon, phases and eclipses
sections.text:
The Moon shines by reflected sunlight. Half its surface is illuminated at a time, apart from eclipse effects, but the fraction of this sunlit half visible from Earth changes during its orbit. New Moon, crescent, quarter, gibbous and full Moon are viewing geometries. The dark part of a quarter Moon is not normally Earth's shadow.

A solar eclipse occurs when the Moon passes between the Sun and Earth and its shadow reaches Earth. A lunar eclipse occurs when Earth lies between the Sun and Moon and the Moon enters Earth's shadow. Solar eclipses require new Moon; lunar eclipses require full Moon. They do not occur every month because the Moon's orbital plane is inclined relative to Earth's orbital plane. Alignment near the orbital nodes is also needed.

```text
Solar eclipse:  Sun → Moon → Earth   (Moon's shadow falls on Earth)
Lunar eclipse:  Sun → Earth → Moon   (Moon enters Earth's shadow)
Not to scale; the bodies and shadow cones have very different sizes.
```

The umbra is the region of complete blockage of direct sunlight; the penumbra receives only partial blockage. Total, partial and annular solar eclipses depend on alignment and apparent disk sizes. Earth's atmosphere can bend and filter some sunlight into its shadow, helping give the Moon a reddish appearance during a total lunar eclipse.

sections.title: Tides and connected gravitational effects
sections.text:
Tides arise principally from differences in the Moon's gravitational pull across Earth, together with the Earth–Moon system's motion. The Sun also contributes. Water nearer and farther from the Moon responds differently relative to Earth's centre, producing a tidal pattern that is modified strongly by coastlines, basin shape and water depth.

Spring tides occur near new and full Moon when lunar and solar tidal effects reinforce one another. Neap tides occur near quarter phases when their effects partly offset. “Spring” refers to a larger tidal range rather than the season. Actual tide timing and height require local prediction; a simple two-bulge illustration cannot capture every coastal situation.

**Solar and sidereal days.** A sidereal rotation is measured relative to distant stars and lasts about 23 hours 56 minutes. A mean solar day is approximately 24 hours because Earth also advances around the Sun and must rotate slightly farther before the Sun returns to the same meridian. This distinction matters for geostationary satellites: matching a generic 24-hour period without the required geometry would not produce a truly fixed position in the sky.

**The Moon's two familiar monthly periods.** The Moon's orbit relative to the stars takes about 27.3 days, while the new-Moon-to-new-Moon cycle takes about 29.5 days because Earth moves along its own orbit. The Moon's rotation is approximately synchronized with its orbital period, which is why roughly the same hemisphere faces Earth. The far side is not permanently dark: it receives sunlight during its own cycle. Slight variations in viewing geometry, called libration, allow more than half the lunar surface to be seen over time.

**Habitability and comparative planets.** Earth's liquid water, atmosphere and long-term geological processes support known life. Venus demonstrates the importance of atmospheric composition and energy balance, while Mars illustrates a different history of atmosphere and surface water. A planet's distance from the Sun is relevant but insufficient to establish habitability: pressure, chemistry, geological activity and radiation environment also matter. Discovering a planet in a nominal habitable zone does not prove the existence of life.

questions.prompt: Why is the Northern Hemisphere tilted toward the Sun during its astronomical summer?

options.A: Earth is always closest to the Sun in northern summer
options.B: The Moon provides more heat than the Sun
options.D: Earth's tilted rotational axis maintains its orientation approximately as Earth revolves around the Sun

questions.explanation: Axial tilt and revolution change the Sun's apparent height and day length, producing seasons.

questions.prompt: A new Moon occurs, but observers see no solar eclipse. The most important explanation is:

options.A: The Sun produces no visible radiation
options.B: The Moon's orbital plane is inclined relative to Earth's orbital plane
options.C: New Moon occurs only once per decade

questions.explanation: The Moon's approximately five-degree orbital inclination normally prevents precise eclipse alignment.

questions.prompt: For otherwise similar circular orbits around Earth, which satellite generally has the higher orbital speed?

options.C: The satellite at the smaller orbital radius
options.D: The satellite with the brighter photograph

questions.explanation: Circular orbital speed follows v = sqrt(GM/r), so a smaller orbital radius implies a higher speed.

questions.prompt: According to Kepler's second law, a planet traveling in an elliptical orbit sweeps equal areas in equal times. It therefore generally moves:

options.B: Fastest when farthest from the Sun
options.D: Only when the Sun is above the horizon

questions.explanation: Conservation of orbital angular momentum is associated with faster motion near perihelion and slower motion near aphelion.

questions.prompt: Why does a half Moon appear partly dark even when Earth's shadow is not covering it?

options.A: The observer sees only a portion of the Moon's sunlit hemisphere
options.B: The Moon loses half its surface every month
options.C: The Sun stops illuminating the Moon
options.D: The dark portion is always Earth's eclipse shadow

questions.explanation: Ordinary lunar phases arise from viewing geometry: the Moon's sunlit half is seen from different angles during its orbit.

questions.prompt: Which phenomenon is directly associated with Earth's axial tilt and high-latitude summer illumination?

options.D: The midnight Sun above polar circles

questions.explanation: Near polar regions, axial tilt can keep the Sun above the horizon for an entire day or longer during the relevant summer season.
